newsitem.title: USA: Homestake Mining to buy Santa Fe Pacific Gold.
newsitem.headline: Homestake Mining to buy Santa Fe Pacific Gold.

text.p: Homestake Mining Co. agreed to buy Santa Fe Pacific Gold Corp. for $2.3 billion, outbidding Newmont Mining Corp. and creating the second largest gold producer in North America, the companies said Monday.
Under the terms of an agreement approved by the boards of both companies, Santa Fe shareholders will receive 1.115 newly issued Homestake common shares for each Santa Fe common share.
Each Santa Fe share would be worth $17.42 share, based on Homestake's closing stock price Friday.
The agreement was signed just days after Newmont Mining disclosed a $2 billion unsolicited bid for Santa Fe. Newmont's all-stock bid was valued at $15.55 a share.
Santa Fe shares closed Friday at $15.25; Newmont at $46.875; and Homestake at $15.625.
Stock analysts had said last week that Homestake was a leading candidate to provide an alternative to Newmont's unsolicited bid.
The combined Homestake-Santa Fe operation would have the largest gold reserves and would be the second-leading producer of gold in North America.
Homestake President and Chief Executive Jack E. Thompson will become chairman and chief executive of the new company.
Patrick James, chairman, president and chief executive of Santa Fe, will become president and chief operating officer, the statement said.

"This is an ideal transaction for the shareholders of both companies," Thompson said. "Santa Fe's shareholders get a full and fair price, representing a 47 percent premium to last Wednesday's unaffected market price for their shares, and the potential upside of owning half of a dynamic new gold company."
Homestake's shareholders receive an increased base of U.S. reserves for an effective price of about $125 per ounce of reserves, Thompson added.
The new Homestake, with headquarters in San Francisco and an operating base in northern Nevada, will have eight underground and nine surface mines in four countries.
It said it expects to achieve more than $30 million in annual cost savings by eliminating overlapping expenses and by combining and refocusing its exploration programme, especially in Nevada.
The companies said they will close Santa Fe's Albuquerque, N.M., headquarters and relocate certain members of the management team to San Francisco and Nevada.
The transaction, which is expected to close by early April, is subject to approval by both companies' shareholders, antitrust approval, and other customary conditions.
